newsitem.title: UK: Pressure groups set to exercise greater sway - study.
newsitem.headline: Pressure groups set to exercise greater sway - study.

text.p: European businesses expect the impact of pressure groups on their operations to increase, but warn that some activists' naivety could damage relations, a survey from London-based consultancy Control Risks showed.

The survey of 51 major European companies, published on Monday, said that while 99 percent of businesses said they were keen to collaborate with pressure groups, in reality just one in eight companies has formal procedures to do so.

"They are clearly worried about pressure groups oversimplifying or distorting the facts. But if businesses refuse to enter a dialogue, they cannot realistically expect understanding," said Richard Fenning, development director for Control Risks.

Companies were generally happier dealing with environmental activists than with issues such as corruption, where they were "less comfortable that pressure groups would understand the realities of business".

Governments also have a large impact on business activities such as the U.S. Helms-Burton legislation which can punish companies doing business with Cuba, but their activities are tempered by commercial realism. "Domestic pressure in the U.S. to punish pariah states may produce more legislation along the lines of Helms-Burton. But this willingness will be tempered by a reluctance to jeopardise investment prospects in major markets -- witness the U.S. government's reluctance to link China's human rights record with trade and investment issues," said John Bray, Control Risks' principal research consultant.
Among the European companies surveyed, the British are more sensitive to human rights issues than the Germans or French.

One in three British companies said that it had altered an investment decision because of human rights issue, whereas just one in four French companies and only one in fourteen German companies had done so. Concerns about corruption had also deterred almost half the British respondents, but none of the French and only one of the German companies questioned in the study.
"Under German law, commercial bribes paid abroad are in some circumstances tax-deductable, though this is increasingly a matter for public debate," the study noted.

While there is a recognition by businesses of the value of investing in emerging economies, Control Risks noted that their enthusiasm had been tempered by the complexity of economic and political transition.
"While the political shift often happens very rapidly, there is generally a time lag before legal and commercial structures come into place," Control Risks' Bray said.
"In this fluid and volatile state, pressure groups have a role to play in promoting a sense of corporate and general accountability, before more formal systems can develop."
